  • OpenAI models' Hugging Face breach is a red flag for bankers
  • The top-performing banks with $2B to $10B of assets in 2025
  • Inside Upstart's journey to get a bank charter approval

Every organization has those who are driving it forward. Much as I might like to think it's people like me who are sitting in executive seats, it's not. It's the people doing the selling, implementing and serving. It's people on the front lines. Those are the people who sacrifice the most for arbitrary return-to-office mandates and who are served least by them.

The work they do isn't about water cooler conversation. The work they do is about productivity and customer connection. That doesn't happen because someone knows Stacy's favorite cocktail is made with bourbon (which is it, and cheers). It happens because they're well equipped to do the job you need them to do; they have quality communication with leadership about why they're doing it; and their contributions are visible and understood beyond who happens to see them at the coffee machine each day.

I won't claim that satisfying each of those conditions is easy. In fact, it's incredibly hard. However, every minute wasted on counting badge swipes or debating whether three days a week in the office is best, or should it be four, is time not spent on creating those conditions.

Return-to-office mandates are chosen stress, and it's an unworthy choice because banking is a very difficult business. Margins have done nothing but shrink for 30 years. Today, banks earn 35% less in net interest margin than they did in 1994. Meanwhile, compliance costs have skyrocketed and consumer expectations for digital delivery have only grown. Those are long-term dynamics. Now, add the near-term challenges of markets whipsawing from one social media post to the next, and "unprecedented" conditions occurring so often the word has lost all meaning.

That's stressful. Stress that is happening to us, not by us. In that environment, why would a financial institution choose the stress created by return-to-office mandates? If you're not convinced by the equity argument, you should be compelled by the financial one.

Don't you need the individuals who are driving you forward to be engaged and stick with you? I know I do, and I know better than to confuse badge swipes with employee engagement. I hope you do too because everyone deserves a working environment that respects equity and rewards strong performance. And fair warning, if you don't deliver that to them, I will. Consider yourself warned.

data.title: German payment startup is close to launching US bank
data.description:
• Key insight: Augustus now has the next U.S. regulatory approval it needs to open its AI-powered international clearing bank.
  • Expert quote: "Innovation-friendly supervision doesn't mean risk-free supervision." —Theodora Lau of Unconventional Ventures
  • Forward look: Augustus President Greg Quarles previously said that the bank is aiming to open in Q3 of this year.

Augustus National Bank is now one step closer to opening to the public and becoming a competitor to some U.S. banks, as it has received official approval from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure its deposits.

Augustus announced this week that its FDIC insurance application was approved on July 31. The renamed German payments startup, which got conditional approval for a de novo bank charter in May of this year, is working to build a digital clearing bank with artificial intelligence and stablecoin rail technology.

Augustus is one of a number of fintech companies to apply for a bank charter from U.S. regulators in recent months. It is seeking to provide international enterprise customers with direct access to U.S. dollars and payment rails for clearing transactions instead of partnering with intermediary banks and fintechs. 

The approval comes shortly after Augustus raised $180 million in a Series B fundraise and achieved unicorn status with a $1 billion valuation.

The FDIC approval filing states that the application is approved subject to various conditions, such as initial paid-in capital funds of no less than $73.7 million.

Theodora Lau, founder of fintech consulting firm Unconventional Ventures, told American Banker that the conditions in the approval are typical for the FDIC.

"The minimum initial capital, standard three-year de novo conditions, management and ownership change approvals and one-year window to open are all fairly consistent with what the FDIC typically imposes on de novo national banks," she said. 

The main unique differentiator in the approval, according to Lau, is a jurisdictional consent requirement for non-U.S. executives at Augustus. The filing stated that proposed bank executives who aren't U.S. citizens or residents will need to sign paperwork from the FDIC agreeing to being under the regulator's supervision.

"The specific callout is interesting," Lau said. "It's a small but important reminder for a foreign-born entity now operating within a U.S. regulatory perimeter."

Read more:

  • Should a bank ever be liable when a customer gets scammed?
  • OpenAI models' Hugging Face breach is a red flag for bankers
  • The top-performing banks with $2B to $10B of assets in 2025
  • Inside Upstart's journey to get a bank charter approval

Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz originally co-founded the bank's parent company in his native Germany as an instant payments fintech called Ivy, which subsequently rebranded to Augustus upon approval of its U.S. bank charter application. Augustus' chief technology officer, Simon Wimmer, is also based out of Germany.

"With this approval, we're one step closer to giving fintechs, banks, businesses and builders around the world direct access to dollar banking infrastructure," Dabitz said in a statement. "We look forward to continuing to work closely with regulators as we build a world-class American bank that brings secure, trusted dollar access to financial institutions globally."

Augustus National Bank President Greg Quarles previously told American Banker in May that the bank's executive team is aiming to open its doors later this year.

"We're trying to work for a Q3 opening just like Erebor did," Quarles said at the time. 

Lau said that the FDIC approval shows that regulators are open to new models and are "pricing the novelty in capital, governance control and supervisory oversight instructions.

"Innovation-friendly supervision doesn't mean risk-free supervision," she said.

data.title: CRA proposal may strain banks' relationships with nonprofits
data.description:
• Key insight: A proposal from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. would limit the proportion of nonprofit administrative expenses on Community Reinvestment Act-qualified grants to 15% and heighten scrutiny of community development donations.
  • Supporting data: Grants and donations are a relatively small part of CRA-qualified investments, but many organizations rely on them for funding.
  • Forward look: The proposal is likely to trigger a debate during the forthcoming 60-day comment period.

Banking regulators' latest attempt to rewrite regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act include new restrictions on grants banks give to nonprofits as part of their strategies to meet the needs of underserved local communities.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on Friday proposed relieving banks under $10 billion in assets from full CRA data and reporting requirements as well as narrowing what counts as "credit" on firms' community reinvestment report cards. 

Banks currently can satisfy their CRA obligations by lending to or investing in organizations that work in areas like affordable housing or community development. They can also give grants or donations to nonprofits with similar missions and obtain CRA credit for those contributions. The proposal, by contrast, would credit banks only for grants where no more than 15% goes to the nonprofit's operating costs — a standard that is in line with the default overhead cap that applies to reimbursement for government grants, as outlined in guidance from the Office of Management and Budget.

The agencies say the proposal is meant to shift the law's focus toward lending to communities themselves and away from funding the community reinvestment industry. 

Both the first Trump administration and Biden administrations put forward overhauls to the CRA framework, but each effort was scuttled by the following administration, leaving the 1995 regulations in place.

"The agencies believe this … requirement will help ensure the vast majority of community development grant dollars are used to benefit the large bank's assessment area, rather than the organization administering the community development program, project, or initiative," the proposal states. "The agencies also believe this requirement would better prevent rent extraction and ensure the vast majority of grant funds are provided directly to the large bank's local communities."

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould characterized the recent proposal as an effort to refocus CRA on its statutory purpose, saying the changes would prevent the law from being used "as a social credit score for banks" or "as a funding mechanism for activist NGO networks under the guise of community development."

The proposal also limits grants that qualify for CRA credit to community development programs in the bank's geographic area. Currently banks can earn credit for grants to nationwide organizations. 

Jeannine Jacokes, CEO and founder of Partners for the Common Good, said the change appears targeted primarily at larger banks that make more substantial grants to community organizations.

"It appears as though the grant provisions are really targeting the largest banks," Jacokes said. "If a nonprofit organization [is] based in Washington, D.C., and a large bank doesn't have Washington, D.C., in their assessment area, that large bank, if they gave the organization a grant, could not get CRA credit for it. … It would disincentivize any activities if they were not in the bank's assessment area."

Jacokes said many smaller banks already provide relatively limited grant funding, often to highly local organizations. But she said the proposal could constrain large banks' ability to provide flexible operating support.

Read more:

  • Should a bank ever be liable when a customer gets scammed?
  • OpenAI models' Hugging Face breach is a red flag for bankers
  • The top-performing banks with $2B to $10B of assets in 2025
  • Inside Upstart's journey to get a bank charter approval

"It's quite clear that [the agencies are] not interested in supporting general operating costs," she said. "That's what the big change is."

Ken Thomas, a longtime CRA consultant and expert, said the proposal represents a meaningful departure from the current framework because it moves beyond evaluating whether a grant serves a community development purpose and instead scrutinizes how recipients spend the money.

Thomas said the changes could reshape which organizations receive CRA-supported funding, potentially favoring smaller organizations with narrowly defined projects, "while making it more difficult for larger … national organizations engaged in advocacy, research, coalition building, or broader community development work to qualify for CRA-supported funding.

"Many legitimate nonprofits, especially smaller grassroots nonprofits, have indirect costs above 15%, often in the 20-25% range," Thomas added. "The requirement will likely cause banks to scrutinize grant recipients much more carefully before making CRA-qualified contributions."

Grants and donations make up a relatively small share of banks' overall CRA-qualified investments, the overwhelming majority of which are spent on development projects. Even so, nonprofit advocates argue the significance of grants extends beyond their dollar share because they often provide flexible funding that allows community organizations to operate. 

The proposal would make a historically flexible area of CRA compliance substantially more complicated, according to James Wylie, vice president of public policy and senior fair lending counsel at the National Fair Housing Alliance.

"The rule before [was] extremely flexible on what counted as a community development grant," Wylie said. "This makes something that was quite easy to do before, potentially, quite hard."

Wylie said banks generally respond cautiously to new compliance requirements and may become more selective about which organizations they support.

"This is going to impact the funds that community nonprofits have available in the housing and community development space," Wylie said. "Groups have already had to lay off staff; they've already had to forgo programs. So it is a real challenge."

data.title: How better understanding brain science can boost advisors' business
data.description:
Financial planner Vanessa Martinez kicked off a discussion about the emotional, neurological and psychological sides of the profession with a simple question: How many audience members had experienced a client crying in a meeting? 

Many attendees raised their hands during the session at The American College of Financial Services' Conference of African American Financial Professionals this week in Chicago. For the few who didn't,  Martinez called them "very brave" and posed a challenging follow-up: "Did you not notice that it was about to happen, or did you stop it from happening?"

Martinez, the CEO and founder of Chicago-based registered investment advisory firm Expressive Wealth and a co-founder of the SER Summit for Latinos in Financial Services, said financial triggers can be anything related to money and wealth — anything that makes them think about what is really happening in their lives. While many advisors may resist allowing clients to be so vulnerable, she said advisors have no choice but to study such emotions. 

"I know there are many advisors that think, 'No, that's going too far. I don't want to get in that type of relationship with my clients,'" she said. "The issue is you are, regardless of if you want to or not."

Questioning the conventional approach

Acknowledging and learning about these aspects of planning represents an important aspect of professional and business growth for advisors, according to Martinez and her sister, Patricia Villarreal, the founder and executive director of therapy provider Holding Space for Psychological Wellness, as well as the chief clinical officer for Martinez' firm. 

For some advisors, that means grasping key neurological concepts, engaging in a little self-reflection and outright rejecting the industry's conventional approach.

For instance, Villarreal has held that novel advisory practice role of "chief clinical officer" since Martinez launched her RIA about two years ago, adding her psychological background to client meetings in a way that her sister views as providing a better understanding for everyone involved of the underlying dynamics at play with tough topics like death, divorce or inheritance. She and Martinez weren't suggesting advisors become psychologists. 

Rather, some basic knowledge about "the neuroscience of what's happening, almost reflexively, in our bodies as we walk into a room, especially when we're talking about such a loaded topic like finances," can inform advisors' service to clients and help their business, Villarreal said.

"Most people make decisions based on emotion, and that informs how they determine the logic in their decision making," she said. "Yes, we may be emotionally driven, and so maybe the person sitting right across from you will be a very emotionally driven person. But that doesn't mean that it's not a logical decision that they're making." 

By communicating more deliberately and providing analytical clarity, advisors can better connect with the emotional side of a client's decisionmaking process in a way they previously may not have been ready to do.

The financial side of the brain

More advisors are seeking training to build skills in the many psychological aspects that fall under the common umbrella term "behavioral finance." The CFP Board added the psychology of planning to its list of principal topics covered by its examination five years ago, and advisors might consider pursuing the "certified financial therapist" designation among other resources.  

Martinez and Villareal's presentation offered advisors some practical advice to keep handy in the meantime. They shared five "communication habits of elite advisors," which called for planners to ask better questions, listen more closely, speak "second or last," slow down and sum up the most important takeaways for clients. To make that list more succinct, one of the last slides of the talk included the contention that, for advisors, "The questions you ask can demonstrate your intelligence more than the answers you give."    

Villareal took that discussion even deeper by explaining the intersection of financial advice with the parts of the brain called the amygdala and the mirror neurons, as well as the hormones of cortisol and oxytocin. The amygdala is "the part of our brain system that is most impacted by trauma" and the section "that stamps emotion to our memories," she said. 

"I'm not suggesting that we need to think through a 20 million-line checklist of how we can potentially prepare for that, so that we can be as neutral as possible, because that's not realistic," Villareal said. "However, we do need to consider that things as small as a scent, a candle burning in the background —  whatever it is, what I'm wearing today, how I'm greeting someone — can impact someone's openness and their feeling of safety, depending on their lived experience." 

For some clients, she said, talking about money may not feel safe because of how they grew up or because of negative experiences with a previous advisor.

To round out the other concepts, Villareal said that cortisol is "a stress-managing hormone" that is "very helpful in moderate doses, but, when we're living in chronically stressful environments, can be destructive for us, can cause a lot of health complications for us." Oxytocin is a "hormone most commonly experienced by birthing women, nursing women and in loving relationships," that can occur in micro doses in situations where someone feels safe and loved. It can also help people develop trusting relationships. And scientific studies suggest mirror neurons are "the reason that we are able to feel empathy in a room across from someone — when someone is having some kind of painful experience, we can almost put ourselves in their shoes."

By way of explanation, she returned to Martinez's example of a client crying in a meeting and the possible concerns advisors may have about that. 

"Well, we don't want to embarrass this person, make them cry, so I'll change the topic in order to be able to lessen their felt sense of embarrassment," Villareal said. "Is that about them, or is that about us, in our discomfort with whatever may be happening across from us? That's what we have to ask ourselves." 

It's important for advisors to understand the "why" behind those choices, she said. And recognizing the role of the brain and hormones can help advisors improve their own emotional intelligence, self-awareness and self-regulation. 

Business implications of brain science

That level of analysis by advisors about both sides of a client conversation, Villareal and Martinez said, can lead directly to better service to customers and potential business opportunities. In some cases, it calls standard industry approaches to advice into question.

Martinez said that while advisors typically plan for a client's children, they often miss an important part of the planning puzzle: what clients' parents may need. 

"Typically, as advisors, we're like you, your immediate family and down a generation. How many of us go up a generation?" Martinez said. "Who's going to take on the burden of your parents? You. Well, we haven't talked about that. That's not in my plan. So that's a huge piece that we need to talk about — that, as advisors, we're like, 'Insurance, the houses, the retirement accounts, the trust account, the accounts for the kids.' But we're all going to be in a sandwich era at some point."   

In such cases, any hesitation on an advisor's part to discuss everything intertwined with a client's parents may hurt their business amid "the giant wealth transfer happening because of the boomers," Villarreal pointed out. Many advisors could have understandable qualms about broaching the topic of the aging and death of their clients' parents.

"They're going to start needing to care for them," Villarreal said. "They're going to start needing to think about end-of-life things, the stuff that people like to avoid because it's dark and it's morbid and, like, I don't want to be bringing up something that's going to make someone sad again for that same reason. Yes, of course, end-of-life planning is difficult. It's difficult to talk about, especially if someone is anxious to talk about it and you may have already known that or experienced that with that client. But that's especially why we need to be able to lean into that." 

Advisors need curiosity and authenticity, not a doctorate

Advisors can learn more about when they should consider referring clients to a psychiatrist and keep in mind that they "don't need to know everything ahead of time," she said. While they're experts in planning and investing, rather than therapy, no one from any field can present a client with a plan on "how to make your life perfect" through a "step-by-step process" leading to long-term happiness, Villarreal said. But advisors who have cast off some of those doubts about establishing deeper relationships can make a big difference in clients' lives.    

"I think it's critically important to not lose ourselves as a human being in the room across from anybody," she said. "That's a really hard thing to do, to be as authentically ourselves as possible."

For Martinez, two realizations — "We have to be ourselves to be able to connect with other people" and "You have to be curious before you make the conclusion" — came as she advanced in her career. The seemingly unrelated ideas may prove especially challenging for Black, Latino or other minority advisors who are underrepresented in the field.   

"If we are guarded, then it's impossible that I'm going to try to build this trust situation in the room," she said. When she first started as an advisor, she wore pearl earrings instead of her preferred hoops, worried that she didn't look the part. 

"But now I'm like, 'No, I need to be me to let you be you,'" she said. "And that's hard because of the environment that we're in."

Advisors who can conquer those underlying fears and gain more appreciation for the neurological factors related to wealth will stand a better chance of creating multigenerational relationships with families and earning client referrals, Martinez said. She told the story of a client who scaled a steep mountain with friends and, to the friends' surprise, called Martinez from the summit. At that point in a client relationship, referrals have nothing to do with investment or trust strategies.

"We're building these relationships so they're strong enough that, when future things happen, you're still their advisor, you're their kids' advisor and it goes from generation to generation," Martinez said. When a client calls you from a mountaintop, you know you've reached a level of connection that ensures a long relationship. "Those are the real, real, real referrals," she said.

data.title: Mortgage rates keep rising, nearing last July's peak
data.description:
Rates on the conforming 30-year fixed mortgage increased 3 basis points this past week and are now higher on a year-over-year basis, as inflation remains front and center in the minds of investors.

The latest rates have moved closer to their July 2025 level at over 6.7%, although still below the 7% peak they briefly topped in February that year, Freddie Mac reported.

The 30-year FRM averaged 6.69% for Aug. 6, up from last week when it was at 6.66%, the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey found. For this same week last year, the 30-year was 6.63%.

Meanwhile, the 15-year FRM moved lower, to 6.01%, compared with last week's 6.04%. A year ago, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.75%.

"While mortgage rates continue to influence affordability, the housing market is showing signs of adjustment, with listing prices modestly below year-ago levels and for-sale inventory improving from the limited supply seen in recent years," Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist, said in his comments on this week's survey.

Lender Price data posted on the National Mortgage News website had the 30-year FRM product at 6.89%, the first time it fell below 6.9% in several weeks.

The 10-year Treasury yield, a benchmark used to help price mortgages, went from a July 31 close of 4.75% down to 4.62% on Aug. 3. But on Thursday morning, at 11 a.m., it was back up to 4.65%.

Conforming mortgage rates according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's Weekly Application Survey also rose to 6.81% for the period ending July 31, the highest in a year.

Preliminary reports of some progress on the geopolitical front have tempered the rise in daily mortgage rates, said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow Home Loans, in a Wednesday evening statement.

"Still, the backdrop remains complicated — year-over-year comparisons are less favorable than they were, and geopolitical negotiations don't always follow a straight line," Ng said. "Slightly lower mortgage rates in recent days also come amid a divided Fed, whose next move is more likely to be a hike than a cut."

Higher borrowing costs combined with what Ng termed as "tougher year-over-year comparisons" are leading her to predict "a softer second half for housing."

Nigel Green, CEO of the deVere Group, points to market data, which prices the likelihood of a Federal Open Market Committee 25 basis point rate hike in September at over 60%.

This change in sentiment "in a single month tells you the debate inside the Fed has genuinely changed, not just the mood on trading desks," Green said.

The concern is over inflation driven by rising oil prices.

"Officials who felt comfortable holding steady in June are now looking at a very different inflation picture heading into September," Green commented.

data.title: New professional designation aims to build DAF expertise
data.description:
Advisors interested in serving charitably inclined clients will soon have a new designation program to consider, one focused specifically on donor-advised funds.

The nonprofit American College of Financial Services will launch the donor-advised fund certified professional program, on Sept. 1. The 30-hour online curriculum has no prerequisites and can be completed at a self-guided pace over eight to 20 weeks. Tuition is $1,495 for most financial professionals or $1,195 for nonprofit professionals. The King of Prussia, Pennsylvania-based organization offers more than 150 state-approved continuing education courses.

Six modules make up the DAFCP course, covering DAF fundamentals; tax fundamentals; gift acceptance; investing and grantmaking; estate and planned giving; and ethics, compliance and technology.

"Donor-advised funds involve highly complex planning considerations, and financial advisors need specialized knowledge to serve clients, especially high-net-worth individuals, who expect proficiency in this area," Paul M. Caspersen, program director of the new designation program, said in a statement. "For professionals at DAF-sponsoring organizations, the designation offers technical grounding and a mark of ongoing professionalism."

DAFs are one tool among many

Advisors tend to recommend DAFs as a tax-advantaged method of giving so clients can maximize charitable contribution deductions or donate appreciated assets while avoiding capital gains taxes.

"More education is always beneficial, and so if people have time and capacity and interest, I think there's things that would translate through, but you could do it as part of a broader charitable planning section," said Chris Nason, head of private wealth at New York City-based estate and tax planning platform Wealth.com and a lecturer of trusts and estate planning at Stanford Law School. "DAFs are interesting. DAFs are special. DAFs are super important, but they're a tiny slice of charitable giving."

Considerations related to DAFs — such as advising clients, choosing charities and planning the bunching and valuations in how to deploy funds — can be useful in other situations, too, Nason said.

DAFs are just one way of being philanthropic, and it's best to start with "the why," while "DAFs are the 'how,'" said Andrew Slade, VP and endowment and foundation advisory team lead at Philadelphia-based Glenmede, a boutique wealth management firm.

"I wouldn't want advisors who are newer to philanthropy to conclude that DAFs are the only solution or the best one for every client just because they have this designation," he said.

DAFs can help mitigate a downside to charitable giving that resulted from tax law changes. The increase in the standard deduction, under tax laws passed in 2017 and 2025, reduced the incentive to use itemized deductions, such as the one for charitable contributions. DAFs allow donors to group or "bunch" multiple years of gifts into a single tax year for a one-time deduction; the DAF sponsor then doles out the funds over subsequent years.

Slade said he sees potential for nonprofit development professionals to benefit from the designation, based on his conversations with them. 

"They see assets flowing in, and they say, 'How do I access these funds?'" he said. "My hope would be that this designation would give them further insight into how to cultivate and steward supporters who are giving to their nonprofit through a DAF."

Although nonprofits tend to send formal gift acknowledgement letters to DAF sponsors, since DAFs are the legal source of the funds, engaging directly with the individual donor advisors when possible would "be much more effective for donor stewardship purposes," he said.

Forty-two percent of millennials who donated to charities in the last year reported using a DAF, compared to only 13% of Generation Xers and 10% of baby boomers, according to Bloomerang and The Harris Poll.

However, for some, DAFs may have lost some appeal after recent events. Charles Schwab, Fidelity and Vanguard prohibited the DAFs they sponsor from making grants to the Southern Poverty Law Center, The New York Times and other outlets reported.

"Six months ago, I would have told you 99.999% of the time, the DAF is going to listen to your recommendation," Nason said. "There's been a slight movement in the other direction that gets people a little bit worried."

Slade emphasized the importance of educating clients who are would-be donors that they would legally give up control of their assets if they give to donor-advised funds, whereas private foundations allow them to maintain legal control.

DAFs tend to be more useful for ultrahigh net worth individuals.

"Unless you're trying to bunch your charitable contributions or give away highly appreciated stock, most people are just writing checks sort of on an ongoing basis to the charities that they care about and having their funds take effect immediately," Nason said. It is "different in the ultrahigh net worth space, where DAFs are super important."
